definitions.gloss: doyō; 18-day period before each season change
definitions.explanation: In the traditional Japanese calendar, the ~18 days leading up to each new season (spring, summer, autumn, winter). The summer {土用|どよう} is the best known, associated with eating eel.

examples.japanese: {土用|どよう}の{丑|うし}の{日|ひ}にうなぎを{食|た}べる。
examples.english: We eat eel on the Day of the Ox during doyō.

examples.japanese: {土用|どよう}に{入|はい}ると{暑|あつ}さが{本格的|ほんかくてき}になる。
examples.english: Once doyō starts, the heat sets in for real.

examples.japanese: {昔|むかし}は{土用|どよう}の{期間中|きかんちゅう}は{土|つち}を{動|うご}かしてはいけないと{言|い}われていた。
examples.english: In the old days, it was said that you should not disturb the earth during doyō.

notes:
Originates from the traditional five-element calendar. Strictly, there are four {土用|どよう} periods each year, but in modern usage 'doyō' almost always means the summer one in late July to early August.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {土用|どよう}の{丑|うし}の{日|ひ}: 'Day of the Ox' during doyō — the day to eat eel
- {土用|どよう}{入|い}り: the start of a doyō period
- {土用|どよう}{波|なみ}: rough late-summer waves
- {夏|なつ}の{土用|どよう}: summer doyō

CULTURAL NOTE:
The summer {土用|どよう} falls in the hottest part of the year. There is a tradition of eating eel (うなぎ) on the {丑|うし}の{日|ひ} (Day of the Ox) within this period to build stamina against the heat — a custom popularized in the Edo period and still observed today.
